newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: INTERVIEW-Wms de Broe eyeing Lithuanian equities.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Wms de Broe eyeing Lithuanian equities.

text.p: Investment house Williams de Broe says Lithuania outshines its Baltic neighbours for investment potential and that it is eyeing the country's dairy and manufacturing sectors.

"Lithuania is the largest of the Baltic countries and it also has the largest industrial base. On that basis it has quite a lot of potential," Petri Karjalainen, head of Williams de Broe's Baltic division, told Reuters in an interview.
The population of Lithuania is 3.7 million, compared to 1.5 million in Estonia and 2.5 million in Latvia.
Development has been uneven in the Baltics, with Estonia and Latvia more advanced in terms of infrastructure and legal guidelines for foreign investment, Karjalainen said.
"So there are still quite a lot of things to do in Lithuania. From an investment point of view Lithuania has quite a lot to offer at the moment," said Karjalainen.
Karjalainen said Lithuania's transportation, telecoms, energy and small manufacturing companies -- such as Ekranas and Vilniaus Vingis -- were interesting.
"But our favourites are definitely in the banking sector and manufacturing industry," he said.
"The biggest problem in Lithuania is that the companies are out of cash. The operations can be sound but they don't have any working capital," said Karjalainen, who is based in Helsinki.

Williams de Broe, which is majority owned by Belgium's Banque Bruxelles Lambert SA (BBL), is active in all the Baltic stock exchanges. Last year it bought a stake in Estonian drugs company Tallinn Pharmaceutical.
In January it bought a 14 percent stake in Rokishkis Cheese, a leading cheese maker in the Baltic states and Russia.
Karjalainen said Williams de Broe had placed some stakes in the company, which is listed on the Vilnius bourse, with international clients.

"The Lithuanian equity market in general has seen a bit of a correction, and likewise Rokishkis. But we don't look at it that much in the short term. We're basically looking at the potential it has over the medium term," Karjalainen said.
For 1996 Rokishkis posted a net profit of 12.2 million litas, compared to 9.3 million litas a year earlier.
The company's performance had so far met expectations, Karjalainen said, adding that he anticipated a shake-up in Lithuania's dairy sector.
He said that at one time Lithuania was second only to The Netherlands for per capita dairy production.

Some 75 percent of the company's production was exports, Karjalainen said, adding that Rokishkis was setting up distribution centres in St Petersburg, Moscow and Kazakhstan and would start expanding its sales to Russia.
"The problem right now is that they don't have enough capacity because they could basically double their sales to the western markets and to the eastern markets."
Securing milk supplies was Rokishkis' main obstacle to expansion, Karjalainen said.
"At the moment there are 44 regional dairy companies in Lithuania and there's going to be a very strong consolidation in that industry," Karjalainen said.
"There's space maybe for five to 10 dairies and this one is by far one of the strongest," he said, adding that Williams de Broe was also looking at other Lithuanian dairy companies.
But Rokishkis would definitely come out as a winner.
"They have one of the strongest balance sheets in the whole sector and at the moment they have very little debt.
"What the company presumably will do is look for debt financing. They have just refinanced their debt from very high levels to very preferable levels," he said.
